newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak FinMin may tax yields on state securities.
newsitem.headline: Slovak FinMin may tax yields on state securities.

text.p: The Slovak finance ministry said on Thursday it planned to tax yields from all types of state securities.
Head of the State Assets and Liabilities Department, Marian Horvath, told Reuters that initial plans foresaw a 25 percent tax on such yields.
"But the extent of the tax is not final, we are now in the stage of discussions," Horvath said, declining to elaborate.
The ministry uses treasury bills and state bonds as the main tools to refinance the state budget deficit. Both T-bills and state bonds currently offer tax-free yields.

Horvath said the ministry was also planning to draft by the end of this year an amendment to a central bank (NBS) law to increase NBS participation in covering the budget deficit by buying state securities.
But he would not say what portion of the deficit should be covered by the central bank.
According to current legislation the NBS can only hold state papers totalling up to five percent of budget revenue of the previous fiscal year. Budget revenues totalled 166.3 billion crowns in 1996.
Local media have said the new law should allow the NBS to hold state papers of an equivalent of 10 percent of budget revenues in the previous year.
"All I can say at the moment is that we want to increase the limit, but it is too early to say whether it will be eight, 10 or even more percent of the revenues.
"We (the ministry) definitely don't want to leave it all on the NBS's shoulders," Horvath said.
Larger central bank participation in deficit covering should help the ministry eliminate the negative effect of high interbank rates on refinancing of the shortfall.

The 1997 state budget plans deficit refinancing at an interest rate of some nine percent. But the ministry has been accepting an average 15 percent yields since the beginning of this year due to a money market liquidity shortage which pushed interbank rates to obove 20 percent and has made deficit covering expensive.
The budget shortfall widened to 17.790 billion crowns as of July 8, 1997, from 7.177 billion crowns in the January-May period of 1997.

Earlier this week the ministry accepted an average yield of 18.196 percent in an auction of its three-week treasury bills, up from from 15.00 percent in the previous auction of similar bills on June 19.
Average yield in an auction of one-year state bonds last Tuesday rose to 17.8 percent from 16.8 percent on July 8. -- Peter Laca, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402
